note: Rows for the /economics watch list, read by src/lib/risk-watch.ts with list "economics". Same rules as risk-watch.json: every number comes from a feed at build time; levels are only levels a linked page or the named source states. group chains sit side by side without arrows. Oil and the 30-year yield stay on /risk/ (their briefs live there); the 10-year and the yield curve live here.

rows.why: Fewer jobs added each month, and more people out of work, would mean the labor market is cooling.
rows.key: Payroll months are first estimates, revised in each of the next two reports. The dashed lines are the prior 3-month average and the August unemployment rate.

steps.title: Jobs added each month

extra.label: Average hourly earnings, over the year

steps.why: The number of jobs employers added or cut, from the payroll survey of businesses.

steps.title: Share of workers without a job

levels.label: Aug 4.1%
levels.quote: The unemployment rate was unchanged at 4.1 percent in August

steps.why: People looking for work as a share of everyone working or looking, from the household survey.

steps.title: New claims for unemployment benefits
steps.why: People filing a first claim for unemployment benefits. It comes out every Thursday, between the monthly reports.

rows.why: Prices compared with a year earlier, against the Fed's 2% target.
rows.key: Core leaves out food and energy, which jump around. The Fed's 2% target is set on PCE; CPI is shown against the same line.

steps.title: The Fed's preferred gauge
steps.tracker: Core PCE prices, over the year

levels.label: 2% target
levels.quote: the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) judges that inflation of 2 percent over the longer run, as measured by the annual change in the price index for personal consumption expenditures, is most consistent with the Federal Reserve's mandate for maximum employment and price stability.

steps.why: Personal consumption expenditures prices, from the Commerce Department. The newest month is revised in the next report.

steps.title: Consumer prices

levels.label: 2% target
levels.quote: the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) judges that inflation of 2 percent over the longer run, as measured by the annual change in the price index for personal consumption expenditures, is most consistent with the Federal Reserve's mandate for maximum employment and price stability.

steps.why: The consumer price index, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. It comes out about two weeks before PCE.

rows.why: What the government pays to borrow for two and ten years, and the gap between them.
rows.key: A basis point is a hundredth of a percent. When the 2-year yield is above the 10-year, the curve is inverted and the gap is below zero.

steps.title: Short-term borrowing
steps.why: Moves with where traders expect the Fed's short-term rate to go.

steps.title: Long-term borrowing

levels.quote: The second is 5% for the 10-year Treasury yield, the rate the government pays to borrow for ten years.

steps.why: A high 10-year yield makes future company profits worth less today, which weighs on stock prices.

steps.title: Ten-year minus two-year
steps.why: A positive gap means lenders want more to tie money up for longer.

rows.why: How far the S&P 500 sits below its 52-week high, and how much of the index a few companies make up.
rows.key: A correction is a 10% drop from the peak. A bear market is a 20% drop.

steps.title: Distance from the peak
steps.why: A 10% drop from the high is a correction and a 20% drop is a bear market. The top-10 share shows how much a few big names carry.
